content: 1. No relapses were observed within the first six months of follow-up. However, residual confounding is likely to persist, particularly given the retrospective nature of the study. 2. The risk of bias was assessed as moderate for time-to-mortality outcomes and serious for all other outcomes. 3. Selection bias was deemed serious. All patients admitted to the School of Tropical Medicine (STM) between January 2005 and February 2015 with visceral leishmaniasis (VL) were retrospectively included in the study. 4. Records of HIV-VL patients who were offered secondary prophylaxis were documented, including details on the drugs, doses, and duration of secondary prophylaxis. 5. It is unclear when the follow-up of patients began, as treatment exposure could occur at any time during hospitalization, and analysis was conducted after the study's completion. This introduces a risk of immortal time bias, which was not controlled for. 6. Bias in the classification of interventions was considered low. Hospital records of routinely collected data during inpatient management were analyzed with appropriate permissions. Treatment groups were classified using clearly defined criteria (receipt vs. non-receipt of secondary prophylaxis). 7. There was insufficient information to assess whether deviations from the intended intervention occurred beyond what would be expected in usual practice. All patients received antiretroviral therapy during follow-up, but no information was available on other co-interventions during the 20-year data collection period. 8. Bias due to missing data was considered low. Data were missing for 5 out of 56 patients (9%) initially included in the study. Three patients were lost to follow-up before initiating secondary prophylaxis, and two died during initial treatment before starting secondary prophylaxis. 9. Bias in the measurement of outcomes was considered low. Retrospective data collection from hospital records suggests that outcome measurements were unlikely to be biased by the intervention. 10. Bias in the selection of reported results was assessed as moderate. Outcomes and analyses were clearly defined in the Methods section, but there was no pre-registered protocol or statistical analysis plan available. 11. Combination therapy with liposomal amphotericin B and oral miltefosine was compared to monotherapy with liposomal amphotericin B in various analyses. These included all-cause mortality, clinical cure rates, relapse rates, relapse-free survival, treatment adherence, and adverse events. 12. In Ethiopia, a prospective cohort study of 74 HIV-positive participants receiving pentamidine for VL relapse prevention showed a 7% all-cause mortality rate at two years. Relapse rates were 27% at two years, with a relapse-free survival probability of 79% at six months, 71% at one year, and 53% at two years. 13. Adherence to secondary prophylaxis was 55%, with 41 out of 74 participants completing follow-up and taking at least 11 of the planned 12 doses without experiencing relapse, death, or drug-related serious adverse events (SAEs). 14. During the 12-month follow-up, 21 serious adverse events were reported in 17 out of 74 patients. Two cases of renal failure, potentially related to pentamidine, were observed in patients hospitalized with pneumonia. 15. In South Asia, combination therapy with liposomal amphotericin B and oral miltefosine was evaluated in a non-comparative randomized controlled trial (RCT) involving 150 participants. Clinical cure rates at day 29 were 95%, and relapse-free survival at 12 months was 53%. 16. The combination therapy of liposomal amphotericin B and miltefosine appears to enhance treatment effectiveness and may delay the onset of drug unresponsiveness in HIV-VL co-infected patients. 17. Failure to initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) and concurrent tuberculosis were identified as independent risk factors for poor outcomes in HIV-VL co-infected patients. 18. The GRADE Working Group assessed the certainty of evidence as low to moderate, with downgrades due to study design limitations, imprecision, and insufficient power to detect differences between groups. 19. Combination therapy of liposomal amphotericin B and miltefosine was found to be safe and effective among HIV-VL co-infected patients under programmatic conditions in both East Africa and South Asia.
